The words

Christian soldiers in the conflict!
Bear the banner of the cross;
Rich reward shall crown the victor,
More than recompense for loss.

Not with paltry palms that wither
Shall the brow be gaily crowned,
But with light that shines eternal,
And with heavenly joy renowned.

Yours are mansions fair and comely—
There your souls in bliss shall rest;
Stars shall sparkle in their radiance,
On the pathway of the blest.

Earthly joys are faint and fleeting,
Earthly favours quickly fade;
Heavenwards lift your eyes, expecting
There your true reward is laid.

God be praised who crowns the victor,
Christ be praised who saves from sin;
Equal praise to God the Spirit,
By whose aid we fight and win.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (F♯).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

John Brownlie translated these words from the Latin hymns of the early Church for Hymns of the Early Church (London, 1896), headed “_All Saints_”.

The book printed the words without tunes. They are in Eights and Sevens (8.7.8.7), and this page sets them to ALL FOR JESUS; any other Eights and Sevens tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Traditional Latin
  • Translated (1896): John Brownlie (1857–1925)
  • Music (1887): John Stainer (1840–1901)

Tune ALL FOR JESUS by John Stainer (1840–1901); words by Traditional Latin; translated by John Brownlie (1857–1925).

Sung to the same tune: Brother, Rest from Sin and Sorrow, Come Ye People, Come Adore Him, Fare Thee Well, Our Fondly Cherished, Father, Source of Every Blessing, In the Cross of Christ I Glory, Israel's Shepherd, Guide Me, Feed Me, Israel's Shepherd, Guide Us, Feed Us, Lamb of God, We Fall Before Thee, Light Serene of Holy Glory, One Sweet Flower Has Drooped and Faded, Savior, All My Sins Confessing, Saviour! I My Cross Have Taken, Sister, Thou Wast Mild and Lovely, Theories, Which Thousands Cherish.

Questions about Christian Soldiers in the Conflict

What is the doh of Christian Soldiers in the Conflict?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Christian Soldiers in the Conflict start on?

It starts on m (F♯ in D major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Christian Soldiers in the Conflict in the public domain?

Yes. John Brownlie died in 1925, John Stainer died in 1901; the words were in print by 1896 and the music in 1887. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
